intro: Each passage is a student's answer with two or three mistakes planted in it. Tap every part you think is wrong, then check. Reading like a marker is a quick way to find out what you really know.

segments.t: The word democracy comes from Greek words meaning rule by the people.
In ancient Athens every adult who lived in the city could speak and vote in the assembly,
segments.fix: Only free adult men who were citizens of Athens could take part. Women, enslaved people and people born elsewhere were shut out.
segments.why: Athens introduced the idea that citizens should have a say, but it gave that say to a small group.

segments.t: which made Athens a direct democracy.
Australia is a direct democracy too, because Australians make the laws themselves.
segments.fix: Australia is a representative democracy. Australians choose members of Parliament, who make the laws for them.
segments.why: The only time Australians vote directly on a question is a referendum, and that is about changing the Constitution, not ordinary laws.

segments.t: Power changes hands peacefully when voters choose a different party at the next election.
In a democracy power comes from the people, who choose their government in free and fair elections.
Once a party wins, it can stay in power for as long as it likes without facing the voters again.
segments.fix: Elections must be held regularly, and the losing side hands over power peacefully.
segments.why: A government that never has to face voters again cannot be removed by them, so the people no longer rule.

segments.t: People are free to express their opinions, including disagreement with the government, without being punished.
The rule of law means ordinary people must follow the law, while the people who make the laws do not have to.
segments.fix: The rule of law means everyone must follow the law, including the people who make it.
segments.why: If law-makers were above the law, they could use their power however they liked. Courts can rule against a government, and the government must obey.

segments.t: Citizens can take part between elections by joining campaigns and contacting their representatives.
The Constitution came into effect on 1 January 1901, when the six colonies joined to form the Commonwealth of Australia.
Australia has a federal system, so law-making power is divided between the federal government and the states and territories.
The federal government runs government schools and the police,
segments.fix: State and territory governments run government schools and the police.
segments.why: The federal government looks after matters that affect the whole country. Schools and policing are organised state by state.

segments.t: while the states look after defence and immigration.
segments.fix: Defence and immigration are federal responsibilities.
segments.why: A country needs one defence force and one set of rules about who may enter it, so these belong to the national government.

segments.t: Local councils are set up by state and territory governments and provide services for their local area.
If a state law clashes with a federal law in an area where both can make laws, the state law wins.
segments.fix: The federal law wins.
segments.why: The Constitution gives federal law priority where the two conflict in a shared area.

segments.t: The separation of powers divides government power between three branches so that no single group controls everything.
The legislature is Parliament, which makes and changes laws.
The executive includes the Prime Minister, the ministers and the government departments,
and its main job is to decide court cases.
segments.fix: The executive puts laws into action and runs the day-to-day work of government. Deciding cases is the judiciary's job.
segments.why: Each branch has a different role. Swapping the roles of the executive and the judiciary is the most common slip on this topic.

segments.t: If Parliament dislikes a court's decision, it can order the judge to change it.
segments.fix: Judges decide cases independently. Parliament can change the law for the future, but it cannot direct a judge's decision.
segments.why: An independent judiciary is what allows courts to rule against the government when it breaks the law.

segments.t: In Australia the branches overlap a little, because ministers sit in Parliament as well as running departments. Only the courts stand fully apart.
The federal Parliament is made up of the House of Representatives, the Senate and the King, represented by the Governor-General.
A bill becomes law as soon as the House of Representatives has voted for it.
segments.fix: A bill must pass both the House of Representatives and the Senate, then receive royal assent from the Governor-General, before it becomes law.
segments.why: Both houses must agree. The Senate can amend or reject a bill the House has passed.

segments.t: Parliamentary committees can examine a proposed law and recommend changes.
Government is formed in the Senate by the party with the most senators.
segments.fix: Government is formed in the House of Representatives, by the party or coalition with the support of more than half its members.
segments.why: The Senate reviews laws. It does not decide who governs.

segments.t: The leader of the governing party usually becomes Prime Minister.
Citizenship is a person's formal legal membership of Australia.
National identity is just another word for citizenship.
segments.fix: National identity is a person's sense of connection and belonging. Citizenship is legal membership. A person can have one without the other.
segments.why: Someone can feel strongly Australian before they become a citizen, and citizens express what being Australian means in many different ways.

segments.t: Citizens have rights, such as voting and holding an Australian passport, and responsibilities, such as obeying the law and serving on a jury if called.
Voting is optional for citizens once they turn 18.
segments.fix: Australian citizens aged 18 and over must enrol and vote. Voting is a responsibility, not only a right.
segments.why: Australia is one of the few countries where voting is compulsory for citizens.

segments.t: People who migrate here can apply to become citizens, usually sit a citizenship test and make a pledge at a ceremony.
First Nations peoples have lived on and cared for Country for at least 65,000 years.
Australia's national identity is shaped by shared values and history and by many cultures and traditions.
National identity is fixed: it has stayed the same since 1901 and is the same for everyone.
segments.fix: National identity changes over time and is experienced differently by different people.
segments.why: Family, culture, religion, connection to Country and personal experience all shape how people feel they belong, and those have changed a great deal since 1901.

segments.t: British colonisation began in 1788 and introduced British political and legal traditions that still influence Australia.
To be truly Australian a person has to speak only English at home.
segments.fix: People can keep their languages, cultures and religions while sharing Australia's democratic values.
segments.why: Shared values such as freedom, respect, fairness and a fair go are what hold a multicultural society together, not a single language or tradition.

segments.t: Migration has made Australia a multicultural society with many languages and religions.
Civic action is something an individual or group does to influence an issue or improve the community.
A petition with enough signatures forces the government to change its decision.
segments.fix: A petition is a request. It shows decision-makers how many people care about an issue, but they can still say no.
segments.why: A petition's power is persuasion. It is not a vote and it is not binding.

segments.t: Writing to the Member of Parliament who represents your area is one way to have your say.
Peaceful protest is against the law in Australia.
segments.fix: Peaceful protest is a lawful way for citizens to express their views.
segments.why: Freedom of expression and the freedom to gather peacefully are features of a democracy.

segments.t: Civic action works best when it is lawful, well informed and aimed at the level of government that actually makes the decision.
Only adults who can vote are able to take civic action.
segments.fix: Anyone can take civic action, including young people, by writing to representatives, starting petitions and running campaigns.
segments.why: Voting is one form of participation. It is not the only one.

segments.t: Laws are formal rules made and enforced by legal authorities, unlike the rules of a school or a club.
An effective law is known, clear, enforceable, stable and reflects society's values.
Once a law is made it must never be changed, however much society's views shift.
segments.fix: Laws should be stable, so people know where they stand, but they must be able to change when society's values change.
segments.why: Stable does not mean frozen. A law that no longer matches what the community believes stops being respected.

segments.t: People cannot be expected to follow a law they do not know exists.
A law written in complicated legal language is fine, because only lawyers need to understand it.
segments.fix: A law needs to be clear to the people who have to follow it, not only to lawyers.
segments.why: If ordinary people cannot work out what is allowed, they cannot obey the law, and it will be applied unevenly.

segments.t: In 1970 Victoria became the first place in the world to make wearing a seatbelt compulsory.
The road toll rose sharply in the year after the law came in.
segments.fix: The road toll fell, from 1,061 deaths in 1970 to 923 in 1971.
segments.why: Wearing a seatbelt roughly halves the risk of death or serious injury in a crash.

segments.t: Some people opposed the law because they believed the government should not tell them what to do inside their own cars.
Today wearing a seatbelt is widely accepted, so the law reflects society's values.
The law is unenforceable, because police have no way of telling who is wearing a seatbelt.
segments.fix: The law is enforceable. Police can see whether a seatbelt is worn and issue a fine.
segments.why: Enforceable means the authorities can tell when the law is broken and apply a consequence.

segments.t: The three principles of justice are fairness, equality and access.
Fairness means the judge should decide quickly, based on which side has the better lawyer.
segments.fix: Fairness means impartial processes: the decision-maker has no bias, and each side gets a fair chance to put its case.
segments.why: A quick decision that favours the stronger lawyer is not a fair process.

segments.t: Equality means the same laws apply to everyone, whoever they are.
Access means people can reach and make sense of the legal system, whatever their money, language or location.
Equity and equality mean the same thing.
segments.fix: Equality is treating everyone the same. Equity is giving extra support to those who need it, so that everyone has a fair chance.
segments.why: The two are easy to confuse. Treating everyone identically can still leave some people unable to take part.

segments.t: A political party is an organised group of people who share similar ideas about how Australia should be governed.
A policy is a party's plan for dealing with an issue, such as the cost of childcare.
A party needs the support of more than half the House of Representatives to form government.
If no party wins a majority, a new election must be held straight away.
segments.fix: A party can form a minority government with the support of crossbench members, or parties can agree to a coalition.
segments.why: A hung parliament is resolved by negotiation, not by another election.

segments.t: The Opposition is made up of the independents and the minor parties.
segments.fix: The Opposition is the largest party or coalition outside government. Minor-party members and independents usually sit on the crossbench.
segments.why: The crossbench sits outside both the government and the Opposition.

segments.t: Parties in a coalition work together while keeping their separate identities.

items.title: After the count
items.setup: The House has 150 seats. The Harbour Party wins 70, the Plains Party 62, the Coastal Alliance 11 and independents 7. No parties have agreed to a coalition.

segments.t: With the most seats, Harbour has a majority and will govern on its own.
segments.fix: Seventy seats is fewer than the 76 needed for a majority. Harbour could form a minority government if enough crossbench members agree to support it.
segments.why: Winning the most seats is not the same as winning more than half of them.

segments.t: If Harbour forms government, the Plains Party becomes the Opposition.
The Coastal Alliance members and the independents sit on the crossbench.
The Harbour leader becomes Prime Minister automatically once the count is finished.
segments.fix: A leader becomes Prime Minister once their party can show it has the support of a majority in the House. In a hung parliament that takes negotiation with the crossbench.
segments.why: Nothing happens automatically. The Governor-General commissions the person who can command the House's support.

segments.t: Crossbench members can promise to back the government in Parliament without becoming part of it.
